price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

methodological_questions: Does adherence to a recommended play-type mix predict game or series wins beyond team quality?
Is the recommendation derived independently of the outcome (no outcome-derived label or lookahead)?
Are play-type labels and the suppression trigger measured reliably?
Does the effect survive out-of-sample validation and placebo recommendations?

historical_evidence.finding: Engine top recommended play type beat the team's modal play type in 37/53 series (69.8%) in the full-calibrated headline. Banned-PT (DRIVE-modal) comparisons were 12/14, clean comparisons 25/39 (64.1%), and the uncalibrated archival run was 51.7% (31/60). No bootstrap CI was computed. Recorded failure mechanism is C_artifact, limited by small sample, with LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD and SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER risks.

Ranked playsheet validation on 10 series. Spearman rho=-0.0639 (p=0.0997, n=665) gave no clear full-rank signal. Pairwise Mann-Whitney BEST 1.257 PPP (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 (n=160), p=0.004. Recorded limits are leakage, low measurement reliability and small sample, with drift risk.

Possession-level test of a proxy matchup-conditioned play-type picker on all regular-season games. Effects were +0.047 to +0.0714 PPP with p<10^-3 or smaller on 16,921 cells. The proxy agreed with the production engine only 16.5% of the time, regular-season aggregates were contaminated in-sample, SEs assumed iid, and coverage was 35.7% clear, 33.8% ambiguous and 30.4% no recommendation.
The Possession Control Index gain over ORtg (dR2=+0.139) was leakage tracking DRtg (corr +0.894). Offensive-control components added only +0.005 R2. The baseline omitted defense by construction.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Headline hit rate of the engine's recommended play type vs the team's modal play type, scored at series level
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as C_artifact. Calibration and banned-PT comparisons inflated the rate, leakage/lookahead was present, n=53 was small, and the uncalibrated rate was about 52%.
Recorded limits: leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample. The full-rank correlation was null and only the BEST vs AVOID contrast was significant.
Proxy fidelity was 16.5%, regular-season aggregates were contaminated in-sample, and iid standard errors overstated precision.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Composite index claiming incremental explanatory power over ORtg
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as C_artifact: a mechanical identity/leakage tied to DRtg, not a new signal.

evidence_establishes: Earlier attempts to validate recommended play-type mixes at series level were limited by small samples, leakage or lookahead, and low measurement reliability (FAM:SF-APPS-003, FAM:SF-APPS-018).
The headline 69.8% hit rate (FAM:SF-APPS-003) is recorded as an artifact. The uncalibrated version was 51.7%, close to chance.
A within-half BEST>AVOID contrast on realised play-type PPP (FAM:SF-APPS-018) and a possession-level PPP gain (FAM:SF37) were recorded, but both as inconclusive.
Constructed indices correlated with outcome-defining quantities can show large gains that are mechanical (FAM:SF-APPS-068).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adherence to a recommendation fixed before the game predicts winning (game or series) once team strength is controlled.
Whether any effect on play-type PPP translates into wins.
Any out-of-sample, pre-registered test of adherence, since none of the returned records tests adherence as the exposure.
The effect of the current recommendation engine on 2025-26 data.
own_inferences: As posed, the question is likely to be contaminated by outcome-derived labelling. Adhering to high-PPP play types mechanically raises points, and trailing or leading teams change their mix, which creates reverse causality.
Stronger teams probably adhere more because they run better actions, so team quality confounds adherence and winning.
At 54 series with a binary outcome, only a large effect is detectable. Modest true effects would give an inconclusive result.
Since the suppression trigger is conditional, the number of series with real exposure is probably smaller than 54, which makes sparsity worse.
The prior records are about whether recommendations beat modal play types or alternatives, not whether adherence predicts winning, so the prior work only partly bears on this question.
uncertainties: How adherence is defined (share of possessions, distance from the recommended mix, binary compliance) is not specified.
The recommendation engine version and calibration timing are unknown, so independence from outcomes is unverified.
The per-series number of triggered suppression events is unknown.
The 2025-26 playoffs are only partial on the question date, so the out-of-sample hold-out is incomplete.
The returned records are only a subset of the project history; others may be relevant.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I might have proposed a direct series-level test on 54 units. The records show that the series-level approach produced an artifact (FAM:SF-APPS-003), that leakage and low reliability limited the other validations, and that the proxy-engine run was inconclusive, so I require a frozen, outcome-independent recommendation, game-level clustered analysis with team-strength controls, placebo recommendations and a true hold-out. I downgraded my expectation of a clean positive result.

blocking_constraints.text: 54 series gives low power for a binary series outcome. Only very large effects are detectable, and the series count is smaller still among series with triggered suppression.
If the recommended mix or the trigger is calibrated on the same games or series, or if adherence is scored by realised PPP, the test is circular.
The recommendation must use only information available before each game or series, with the engine frozen before the hold-out.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work compared recommended play types against modal or alternative choices, and validated playsheet rankings and possession-level PPP gains. The results were an artifact (SF-APPS-003), inconclusive (SF-APPS-018, SF37), or mechanical (SF-APPS-068). None directly tested whether adherence predicts winning with an outcome-independent recommendation, so the question remains open.

risks.text: Recommendations or adherence defined using realised play-type PPP make adherence a function of scoring, which is the outcome.

A recommendation computed from games in the same series, from calibration on the evaluation set, or from season aggregates containing the test games contaminates the test (flagged in SF-APPS-003, SF-APPS-018 and SF37).
Team quality, opponent quality, home court, score state and injuries drive both adherence and winning. Reverse causality arises because teams change mix when trailing.
54 series, with fewer having real suppression exposure, gives low power and unstable estimates.
Suppression triggers (a play type dropped by at least 0.25 PPP) are rare per team-game, and 30-35% of pairs had no or ambiguous recommendation in SF37.
Play-type labels derived from play-by-play are noisy, and prior records flag low measurement reliability and low proxy fidelity (16.5%).

Play types with higher league-average PPP produce higher scoring regardless of the suppression condition, so adherence can reflect general efficiency. This is similar to the mechanical identity in SF-APPS-068.
Without a placebo recommendation (modal play type, random mix, wrong-opponent recommendation), any adherence-win association cannot be attributed to the suppression-conditional logic.
Play-type mix and league scoring change across 2022-23 to 2025-26, so recommendations may not transfer between seasons.
Several adherence definitions, play types and thresholds could be tried. The analysis must be pre-specified.

design.estimand: Within-game association between pre-game-determined adherence to the frozen suppression-conditional recommended mix and the probability of winning, conditional on team strength and score-state-independent measures. This is the log-odds ratio per 1 SD of adherence, with the series-level association as a secondary estimand. It is predictive, not causal.
design.unit: Primary: team-game in playoff series with at least one triggered suppression event, clustered by series. Secondary: series (up to 54 with the frozen data).
design.sample: Training/calibration: 2022-23 and 2023-24 regular seasons and playoffs. Validation: 2024-25. Locked hold-out: 2025-26 regular season and playoffs, analysed only after the playoffs are complete (data complete from 2026-06-21). The engine, trigger threshold (for example the 0.25 PPP drop), adherence definition and exclusions are frozen before the hold-out is opened. Recommendations for game g use only data from before game g (prior games, prior seasons, and the first-half trigger only for second-half scoring if used).
design.power: 54 series is the limiting factor. Before unblinding, run a simulation-based power analysis using the game-level cluster structure (about 5-6 games per series) and the observed number of triggered events. State the minimum detectable odds ratio. If it is above a plausible effect (OR about 1.3 per SD), label a null as inconclusive, not rejected. Report CIs by cluster bootstrap. No claims from p-values alone.
design.controls: Pre-series net rating or SRS, seed or rating gap, home court, rest, opponent defensive profile, injuries (starters missing), team and opponent fixed effects or random effects, season effects, and pace. Exclude possessions in garbage time or compute adherence on the first N possessions to reduce score-state reverse causality. Adherence is computed from pre-specified play-type labels with an audited label-reliability subsample (target at least 70% agreement with the production engine, given SF37's 16.5%). Do not score adherence by realised PPP.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo recommendations: team modal play type, random mix matched in marginal frequencies, and wrong-opponent recommendation. The real recommendation must beat all of them. (2) Permutation of recommendations across series within season. (3) Negative-control outcome: adherence in the current game should not predict the previous game's result. (4) Check that adherence does not predict wins in games with no suppression trigger (tests general-efficiency mechanical floor). (5) Compare to a baseline model of team strength only and report incremental out-of-sample AUC or log-loss, not R2 on defined quantities.
design.multiplicity: One primary hypothesis (game-level adherence, one adherence definition, one outcome). Secondary analyses (series level, play-type subsets such as CUT/POST_UP/DRIVE, alternative thresholds) are labelled exploratory and corrected by Holm or reported with FDR. All specifications are logged.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if, on the locked hold-out, the primary adherence coefficient is positive with a cluster-bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero after controls, it beats all placebo recommendations, the falsification checks pass, and incremental out-of-sample log-loss improves over the strength-only baseline. Rejected only if the CI excludes the minimum effect of interest at adequate power. Otherwise report inconclusive, or artifact if the effect disappears with leakage-free recommendations or is matched by placebos.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files and the play-type graph database for 2022-23 through 2025-26. Freeze a dated snapshot with hash after 2026-06-21 (2025-26 playoffs complete). Record the engine version and code commit used to generate recommendations, and the label-generation version.

methodological_questions: Does adherence to a recommended play-type mix predict game or series wins?
How is the recommended mix derived and is it independent of the outcome (outcome-derived label, leakage)?
Are play-type possession labels reliable and are results confounded by team quality?
Does out-of-sample validation across seasons hold for suppression-conditional recommendations?
args.query: suppression-conditional recommended mix adherence predicts winning; best/avoid counter strategy against defensive suppression; playoff series; prior study families and failed approaches

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I need to wrap up with a single JSON object, and I'm keeping in mind that the question was posed on 2026-06-16 while the 2025-26 playoffs only finish on 2026-06-21, so the data is partial. I should also name the data version and freeze it, and I'm weighing the four historical records, where two are artifacts and two are inconclusive.

I'm sketching the study design now: the estimand is the within-series difference in win probability tied to how closely a team follows the recommended mix, with the recommendation fixed from prior games only and adjusted for team strength. I'm also weighing the sample size, since 54 series gives little power for anything but a large effect, and an adherence measure that is computed from the same games as the outcome would mechanically inflate results, so I need a pre-registered recommendation instead.

I'm settling on a probability split for the outcomes and a decision: proceed with changes, reframing the test at the game level on a frozen engine and holding out 2025-26, while noting that its playoffs won't finish until 2026-06-21.
